_**User**_

I need to build a web app (a game) and done by next week (short-time).

There is an event called DMASL Summit. The idea is to gamify an experience for the brand called Fanta. The experience is that attendees play this game, earn points and level up. This is by scanning other attendees' lanyards (no QR or anything, just the lanyard badge).

So the idea is that people will sign up (very basic sign up, no verification) and then they can press a button that opens the cam and they scan the badge and collect points. We need to decide the levels but as they get points they level up. Each scan can be like say 5 points. As levels go up, you would need more points to level up. The bar can be called Fantastic bar or something.

The brand integration is when a ID is scanned, ideally it should have an animation and show the Fanta logo with the a wording like "Fanta-stic person detected". We can cycle through 5 different wordings like that.

Detecting the badge is the main thing. I need to first put together a scope of this and a rough timeline. Also I was thinking we get the badge design from them but how can we detect that its a valid badge?

Ask me any questions needed before we make the plan pls.

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The badge sample may not be available until closer to the event.

This is a high-risk project. Detecting unique attendees without QR codes or a pre-event badge sample is unreliable. I need to be upfront about this risk in the plan and propose alternatives.

A peer confirmation flow could work without unique badge IDs. One attendee scans a badge and the app validates it. The badge owner then confirms the match during signup. This avoids relying on unique visual content.

Face detection is a privacy nightmare and was not requested. Hashing photos is too unreliable under changing lighting. The only practical way to uniquely identify someone without unique printed IDs would be a shared app screen, but that does not scan the physical badge itself.

An honor-system name entry is fragile across five hundred attendees. OCRing the badge name is a better path. If the badge design arrives on event day, a custom ML model cannot be trained in time. A generic template-matching approach using color and logo detection is safer. Any unique printed text should be extracted via OCR to verify identity.

If the badge contains no unique printed text, camera-based uniqueness is impossible. The plan must either include a scan handshake or explicitly document this as a blocker.

For the one-week window, the app should validate the badge visually first. Then it runs OCR; if a unique string appears, it hashes it for identity. If OCR fails, the app asks the attendee to hold still or falls back to cooldown-only tracking.

WebRTC or Bluetooth were considered but rejected as too complex.

A concrete one-week flow is now clear. The camera validates the badge visually first. OCR extracts the name. The user then types or corrects it. The app matches that name to registered users. Points are awarded only if the badge has not been scanned before. This closes the gap where badges lack unique printed identifiers.

An admin tool will let the client upload a reference badge image once the design arrives. The camera will detect it by matching features against that reference, checking for Fanta orange color, and optionally using TensorFlow.js object detection. Three to five real badge photos should be uploaded under the venue’s actual lighting on event morning for calibration. The frontend will use Next.js or Vite with React, and Supabase will handle the database, authentication, and live leaderboard updates.

Firebase is a viable alternative to Supabase for anonymous auth, Firestore, and hosting. The camera will use getUserMedia and Canvas. Detection should run entirely on the device to protect privacy and reduce latency. Only the user ID, a hashed badge identifier, a timestamp, and points should be sent to the server. Signup can rely on a display name plus a device-local storage key paired with a server-side user row, with no email verification required. Anti-cheat measures for five hundred simultaneous users still need to be defined.

Anti-cheat rules are taking shape. Each badge ID can only be scanned once per user. Self-scanning is blocked if the badge carries a self-ID. Scans will be rate-limited and rejected when OCR confidence is low.

A tiered XP curve is planned. Levels will scale from 0–20 scans up to higher tiers. A fantastic progress bar will track advancement.

The Fanta animation will use CSS or GSAP for a logo burst. Five copy variants will cycle through the detection screen.

The demo is scheduled for early next week. The full event is likely Wednesday through Friday.

A concrete six-day timeline is set. Days one and two will cover scaffolding, signup, camera access, dummy scans, points, levels, and the leaderboard. Day three will build the detection pipeline with a placeholder badge and an admin upload for the real reference image. Day four will add the brand animation and polish. Day five is reserved for the demo. Days six and seven will handle on-site calibration and any remaining bug fixes.

Several honest risks remain. Unique-person detection is impossible without a unique printed identifier. The detection quality is unknown until the real badge arrives. iOS Safari camera performance and WebGL memory are concerns. Venue lighting will affect accuracy. Five hundred concurrent writes to the database are also risky.

The recommendation is to ask the client for any photo, even a mockup, to begin building the detection pipeline earlier.

A calibration mode will be built if the client cannot provide a badge sample. The app assumes lanyards carry printed names or attendee numbers, since OCR is the most reliable way to identify unique attendees without QR codes. A two-sided scan flow was considered and rejected. A PWA will allow the app to be added to the home screen at the event.

The plan will be structured as an MVP versus stretch scope. It will detail the architecture, the badge detection strategy, fallback methods for unique-person identification, the points and levels system, the timeline, and client dependencies such as brand assets. Fanta orange and logo will be required for the visual branding.

A text-field confirmation step will sit between visual badge validation and point awards. The OCR result will prefill a prompt asking who was met, and the app will match that name against registered users. This keeps uniqueness independent of perfect OCR.

Unregistered attendees will be stored under a normalized name key. Scanning the same unregistered badge twice will not double-count points.

Vite with React and TypeScript is the preferred stack over Next.js for speed. Tesseract.js is too heavy for mobile and will not scale to five hundred phones. Native OCR APIs are unavailable in Safari and Android lacks a reliable browser path. Cloud vision APIs are too expensive and slow for five hundred concurrent users. The plan is to crop the scanned badge to the name region and send that small image to a lightweight external OCR service.

A two-phase detection pipeline is now preferred. The client first validates the badge visually against the reference image. It then crops the likely text region and runs OCR locally or via a lightweight API. Tesseract.js WASM takes two to eight seconds on mobile, which is acceptable for a game scan if a fun Fanta-themed loading animation is shown.

Tesseract.js will be the primary OCR engine to avoid API costs, with cloud OCR kept as a fallback if the demo proves too slow. For validating badges without a reference sample, the app will extract ORB features from three to six uploaded photos and match live camera frames against that template. OpenCV.js in the browser is feasible. A faster alternative is to use Teachable Machine to train a "badge versus not badge" classifier on-site in ten minutes using twenty photos, which works well when the badge design is still unknown.

The calibration workflow will combine template matching and a teachable-machine classifier. Each scan awards five points. Levels will scale from 0 to 320 total points. The five detection phrases are "Fanta-stic person detected," "Orange you glad we met?," "Flavor found," "New Fanta-stic connection," and a fifth variant.

The demo will use a mock orange object instead of real badge detection, while production will switch to calibrated detection after calibration. Privacy is a priority: badge photos should stay off the server and only hashed identifiers should be stored. For the five hundred-user leaderboard, polling or broadcasting only the top twenty scores avoids naive realtime

The Vite project creation was cancelled because the target directory is not empty.

I'll write the files manually instead. Badge mappings are confirmed and will be copied to public/badges/. I'll skip extra ESLint complexity and keep tsconfig simple. The app will be a phone-first Fanta event scanner for Digital Summit Asia, centered on desktop with a device-like frame.

Game logic will be pure TypeScript for easy testing. State will live in React or localStorage, with a tick interval driving the cooldown countdown across Home and Scanner. I'll batch the file writes. The Vite config enables React. Lilita One and Nunito fonts will load via index.html, plus a simple SVG fanta mark. The scan hit overlay will be full-screen orange with bubbles, showing FANTA branding, badge type, score (+15 FIRST SIP or +5), and a continue button.

Level-up overlays will appear after hits and display the new title and continue button. Both overlays will sequence if triggered together. The scan result type will carry points awarded, badge type, level change, and game state. Scan lines will rotate through a stored index. Hourly caps will filter timestamps within the last hour. A reset demo button will be added for testing.

I'll skip default Vite assets and use a richer bubble CSS background animation. The tsconfig will set jsx to react-jsx. I'll update the existing README with brief run instructions rather than adding new markdown files. The App component will initialize state from localStorage and render the main routes.

The App component will manage four top-level states: screen routing, scan hit details, level-up notification, and toast messages. State persists automatically on every change. The scanner displays five cards and disables them during cooldown with a countdown overlay. The home screen features a large SCAN button. Scans performed this hour will be tracked and displayed.

I'll generate the files with PowerShell New-Item and Copy-Item, then run npm install. The visual palette will be dark cola and orange fizz, not a generic purple gradient. A custom FantaLogo SVG wordmark will appear as a bold italic "FANTA" on orange. I'm batching all file writes now while carefully handling Windows paths.

I'm now writing the core game logic. The BadgeType enum and BADGE_TYPES constant map each role to its label and image path. First-of-type tracking will use a collected array of badge types. I'm also starting the getLevelProgress helper to determine the current level from accumulated points.

The level progression helper iterates backward through the LEVELS array to find the current tier and calculates how close the player is to the next one. Each level has a minimum point threshold. Storage will use the key `fanta-poc-v1`.

I'll add a `vite-env.d.ts` for Vite client types

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
The cooldown timer is displaying an incorrect value of 1:12, exceeding the 60-second limit.

Suspecting the cooldown calculation is off by 12 seconds. Resetting state cleared lastScanAt, so the timer should read 60 seconds. Now inspecting formatMs and cooldownRemaining to find the discrepancy.

The 1:12 display likely persists behind the overlay because the page never navigated away. State may have leaked from a prior session; `start()` spreads the full state object, so stale `lastScanAt` or `scansThisHour` values could carry over.

Ruled out clock skew and Date.now errors. The 12-second offset suggests a stale `lastScanAt` from a prior scan that was never cleared.

Confirmed the cooldown should read 60 seconds after resetting and scanning. The 1:12 display is clearly wrong. Suspecting duplicate timers or leftover scanTimestamps from a prior session. Re-examining the start() function to see how state is spread.

Pinpointed the root cause. `start()` spreads the full `state` object, so it captures the prior player's `lastScanAt` and scan timestamps inside its closure. After `reset()` clears the store, `start()` still copies the old AAAA data instead of an empty state. This leaks the previous cooldown and scan history into the new session.

Reconsidering the stale-state theory. `start()` closes over the latest render, so it should hold empty state after reset. The 1:12 display implies roughly 72 seconds remain. `Math.ceil(72000/1000)` equals 72, and 72 divided by 60 is 1 with a remainder of 12. The raw wait time is likely about 72 seconds.

Found the exact mechanism. A stale `useNow` timestamp on the Scanner was captured before the scan. `applyScan` used that stale time as `lastScanAt`. The cooldown formula subtracts this outdated timestamp from the current time, yielding roughly 72 seconds remaining.

The `useNow` hook freezes the timestamp at mount time. The Scanner stays mounted while the user waits, so the frozen time is 12 seconds older than the actual scan time. `applyScan` records this stale timestamp as `lastScanAt`, which inflates the cooldown to 72 seconds.

The stale timestamp is confirmed. Because `useNow` never updates while inactive, it remains frozen at mount time. When the cooldown finally activates, the hook still calculates against that frozen time, adding 12 seconds to the remaining wait and producing the 1:12 display. The fix is to call `setNow(Date.now())` immediately whenever `active` turns true. The same bug exists in the Home component.

Fixing the `useNow` hook now. After that, I will verify the level-up overlay appears correctly after a Guest scan. The overlay is opaque and fully covers the screen, so the stale cooldown reading is not visible. However, the "Keep scanning" text may be clipped at the bottom of the screenshot, suggesting the overlay content could overflow on shorter viewports.

I'll tighten the overlay layout or enable scrolling so the "Keep scanning" text isn't clipped. First I'll click "Keep scanning" to verify the level-up overlay appears, then apply the `useNow` fix.
</details></think>

<think><details><summary>Thought Process</summary>
Implementing a camera viewfinder with capture functionality.

Badge classification will use template matching on cropped frames via canvas, with OCR as confirmation. A fallback type picker, local leaderboard, and PWA manifest are planned. Tesseract.js may be added for OCR, though it could be slow on mobile.

The classifier will compare the bottom 20% of each captured crop against five badge templates. Role labels like GUEST and DELEGATE differ sharply in width and letter pattern, making them easy to distinguish. This logic will live in a new `detectBadge.ts` module.

The classifier will sample the bottom 22% of each crop and template, then run normalized correlation across several vertical offsets to handle imperfect framing. Camera capture will request 1280x720 environment-facing video.

Camera cleanup runs on unmount. Localhost works over HTTPS. The leaderboard stores entries in localStorage as `{id, name, points, updatedAt}` and displays the top 20. A fallback type picker will appear as a collapsible section on the camera screen. The PWA manifest and icons are being added. Next step is reviewing Home.tsx, styles, and storage modules.

The classifier compares the bottom 25% of each crop against the templates, plus a slightly inset version. A normalized cross-correlation threshold of roughly 0.35 will flag a potential badge. Because the five badge types share nearly identical upper cards, the bottom bar is the sole discriminator. The winning template must also exceed the runner-up by a clear margin.

Templates will be cached in a Map to avoid reloading. A "scanning..." state will appear during capture. The camera screen will use a full-screen video shell with a rounded rectangle guide for portrait cards, a hint to align the front of the pass, and a large capture button. If the back of a badge is photographed, the system will prompt the user to flip it.

A cooldown timer overlay will replace the camera view when scanning is blocked. Failed detections freeze the captured frame and present five type buttons with retry. Successful detection returns type, confidence, and reason. The home screen will gain a Board button alongside the scan option.

Implementing a robust detector.

The five badge variants differ only by their bottom role text. I will crop the viewfinder, isolate the bottom ~22% role bar, and compare it across templates using normalized cross-correlation. A quick color check will verify the beige background and dark bottom strip. Desktop testing can use a printed badge or a second screen.

A file upload option will let users verify detection against the actual badge PNGs without needing a physical badge.

Also matching against the full template resized to the bottom band. The crop function will map the frame overlay’s bounding box to the video element’s display area using getBoundingClientRect.

Mapping the frame overlay to the video source is complicated by `object-fit: cover`. The crop function must calculate the exact source rectangle by comparing the video and display aspect ratios, then determining whether the video is wider or taller than the display area.

The crop mapping logic is now complete and will live in detect.ts. For uploaded images, the entire PNG will serve as the crop since it is already a badge. The bottom 20 percent of the source will be compared against the template bottom 20 percent. A playerId field will be added to GameState so resets generate a new identity while allowing multiple sessions per browser.

The leaderboard will persist rows keyed by a stable `playerId` generated via `crypto.randomUUID()` on first signup. State resets will clear the board entirely. A `BOARD_KEY` constant will store entries as `{id, name, points, level, updatedAt}`. The home screen will receive an `onBoard` callback. The leaderboard screen will list scores, show the user's rank, and include a back button. Saving game state will also trigger an upsert to the board.

Adding PWA support. Creating a standalone manifest with an orange F icon. iOS compatibility may require a PNG fallback.

Detection thresholds are set at NCC above 0.55 with a 0.04 margin. Ambiguous matches will prompt the user to choose. Denied camera access will fall back to file upload and a mock picker. Scanner states begin with live.

Scanner states will expand to reading, failed with preview, and camera-error. The Scanner component will be richer and may split CameraView into its own module. A new leaderboard.ts file will handle board persistence. The scanner CSS will switch to a camera-first layout with the video element absolutely positioned behind a relative UI layer.

The scanner UI will stack vertically with a centered viewfinder frame sized at 68% width or 260px, 5:8 aspect ratio, white border, and a dark shadow ring. The capture button will sit at the bottom. A "Reading pass..." overlay will appear during detection. The file upload input will be labeled "Use a photo," and the mock-picker toggle will be collapsed inside a details summary so the camera remains primary. Template images will be loaded via Image or createImageBitmap.

Same-origin badge PNGs avoid CORS issues. Bottom bands will be extracted from each crop and resized to 160 by 48 pixels for faster comparison. All crops will first be scaled to a uniform 200 by 320 portrait canvas before matching.

The classifier will take a 200 by 320 canvas and return the best match. A debug score will appear in the failed state to help tune thresholds. A Leaderboard button will be added above the Start Over button on the home screen.

Restarting Vite should resolve the blank page and orange loading indicator on the new IP.

The orange likely comes from the app's orange radial gradients and dark shell backgrounds. A stale HMR connection or mobile Safari error may also be causing the blank content.

The blank page with orange glow suggests the shell mounts but React crashes during hydration. Mobile Safari may be failing on newer JavaScript APIs like crypto.randomUUID or optional chaining. Alternatively, the Vite client might be connecting to localhost instead of the network IP, causing the JavaScript modules to fail.

A concrete trigger is now clear: `crypto.randomUUID()` inside the `loadState` hook runs synchronously during React initialization. If the browser lacks this API, the entire app crashes before mounting, leaving only the orange body CSS visible. This explains the blank page with the orange glow.

I will add a polyfill for `crypto.randomUUID` to prevent the boot crash. I also need to configure Vite's HMR host explicitly so the websocket connects to the new IP instead of localhost.

The orange glow confirms the server is reachable and CSS loads, while JavaScript crashes. Other suspects include a cached TypeScript module on the phone, a TypeError in App, or React Strict Mode.

I will kill the old Vite process and restart it with `--host` so it binds to the new network interface. I will also set `server.host: true` and `strictPort: true` in the Vite config, plus `hmr.clientPort: 5173` so the HMR websocket connects over the local network. I plan to test the new IP in the IDE browser to verify the fix.

I will add a `newId()` helper that falls back to a timestamp-based ID if `crypto.randomUUID` is missing, replacing the synchronous call that crashes on mobile. I also ruled out `getContext` and `Image.decode()` as boot-time causes. Next I will kill the old Vite process and restart.
</details></think>
